claim: Eleven patients with Parkinson's disease who had undergone deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery of the bilateral subthalamic nucleus (STN) 2–5 days prior to the recordings were enrolled in the study.
source: Eleven patients with Parkinson's disease (PD, ten males, mean disease duration 7.8 years ± 2.9 standard deviation (SD), mean age 56.7 years ± 11.7 SD), who had undergone deep brain stimulation (DBS) surgery of the bilateral subthalamic nucleus (STN) 2–5 days prior to the recordings, were enrolled in the study.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study participants and timing of recordings.

claim: Participants were significantly faster during high compared to low coherence trials (974 ± 302 ms vs. 1478 ± 298 ms).
source: Analysis of reaction times (RT) showed that participants were significantly faster during high compared to low coherence trials (974 ± 302 ms vs. 1478 ± 298 ms, main effect of coherence: F(1,10) = 83.284, p<0.001)
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-test showing significant difference in reaction times between coherence conditions.

claim: Participants were significantly faster when instructed to emphasize speed over accuracy (1146 ± 322 ms vs. 1306 ms ±259 ms).
source: participants were significantly faster during high compared to low coherence trials (974 ± 302 ms vs. 1478 ± 298 ms, main effect of coherence: F(1,10) = 83.284, p<0.001) and when they were instructed to emphasize speed over accuracy (1146 ± 322 ms vs. 1306 ms ±259 ms, main effect of instruction: F(1,10) = 18.172, p=0.002).
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-test showing significant effect of instruction on reaction times.

claim: There was a significant interaction of instruction*coherence on reaction times (F(1,10) = 9.744, p=0.011).
source: In addition, there was a significant interaction of instruction*coherence (F(1,10) = 9.744, p=0.011), since speed instructions led to a stronger decrease in RT during low coherence compared to high coherence (180 ± 137 ms vs. 77 ± 113 ms decrease in RT, t(10) = 2.662, p=0.024).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing interaction effect with F-test and post-hoc t-test.

claim: Accuracy rates were significantly lower during low vs. high coherence trials (73.9% ± 9% vs. 95.7% ± 5.6%).
source: Accuracy rates were significantly lower during low vs. high coherence trials (73.9% ± 9% vs. 95.7% ± 5.6%, main effect of coherence: F(1,10) = 165.107, p<0.001)
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-test showing significant difference in accuracy between coherence conditions.

claim: There was no significant effect of instruction on accuracy rates (83.9% ± 8% during speed vs. 85.7% ± 7% during accuracy instructions).
source: while there was no significant effect of instruction (83.9% ± 8% during speed vs. 85.7% ± 7% during accuracy instructions, F(1,10) = 1.374, p=0.268)
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-test showing no significant effect of instruction on accuracy.

claim: Participants made significantly more errors during slow compared to fast trials after accuracy instructions (16.6% ± 10.4% decrease in accuracy rates during slow responses).
source: In line with this, we found that participants made significantly more errors during slow compared to fast trials after accuracy instructions (16.6% ± 10.4% decrease in accuracy rates during slow responses, t(10) = −4.731, Pcorrected = 0.002), but not during speed instructions (6% ± 17.3%, t(10) = −1.641, Pcorrected = 0.264).
evidence: Statistical analysis with t-test showing significant difference in error rates between slow and fast trials after accuracy instructions.

claim: The drift diffusion model fitted the data well, as indicated by accurate predictions of the observed RT distributions in all four conditions.
source: The model fitted the data well, as indicated by accurate predictions of the observed RT distributions in all four conditions (Figure 2B).
evidence: Reference to Figure 2B showing model fit to observed data.

claim: Trials with low coherence had significantly lower drift rates than trials with high coherence (100% posterior probability).
source: As expected, trials with low coherence had significantly lower drift rates than trials with high coherence (100% posterior probability)
evidence: Bayesian hierarchical drift diffusion model analysis showing effect of coherence on drift rates.

claim: Decision thresholds after speed instructions were significantly lower than after accuracy instructions (>99% posterior probability).
source: decision thresholds after speed instructions were significantly lower than after accuracy instructions (>99% posterior probability, see Figure 2C).
evidence: Bayesian hierarchical drift diffusion model analysis showing effect of instruction on decision thresholds, with reference to Figure 2C.

claim: There was no effect of instruction on drift rates (67% posterior probability).
source: However, there was no effect of instruction on drift rates (67% posterior probability).
evidence: Bayesian hierarchical drift diffusion model analysis showing no significant effect of instruction on drift rates.

claim: The non-decision time was neither modulated by instructions nor coherence (both 75% posterior probability).
source: Similarly, the non-decision time was neither modulated by instructions nor coherence (both 75% posterior probability).
evidence: Bayesian hierarchical drift diffusion model analysis showing no significant effects on non-decision time.

claim: Eighteen healthy age-matched participants were recruited as controls.
source: In order to approximate physiological STN function as well as possible all patients were tested on their normal dopaminergic medication. All patients had a good dopamine response as indicated by a pronounced improvement of motor function after a levodopa challenge in the preoperative assessment (mean improvement in Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale-III 61.9% ± 12.6, see supplementary file 1). Of note, decision thresholds - the main interest of the current study – are not modulated by dopamine in healthy people (Winkel et al., 2012) or PD patients (Huang et al., 2015). To assess whether patients' behavior was comparable to that of healthy controls, we also recruited 18 healthy age-matched control participants (eight males, mean age 60.5 ± 16.1 years).
evidence: Direct statement about recruitment of healthy control participants.

claim: There was no significant age difference between healthy participants and Parkinson's disease patients (t(27) = −0.675, p=0.505).
source: To confirm that the observed behavior in Parkinson's disease patients resembled 'physiological' task performance, we additionally conducted the same task in 18 healthy age-matched participants (age of healthy participants: range 28–75 y, mean age 61 ± 16 y; age of Parkinson's disease patients: range 31–75 y, mean age 57 ± 12 y; difference between groups: t(27) = −0.675, p=0.505).
evidence: Statistical comparison of age between groups using t-test.

claim: In healthy participants, RT were significantly faster in high compared to low coherence trials (652 ± 124 ms vs. 1238 ± 334 ms).
source: In these healthy participants, RT were significantly faster in high compared to low coherence trials (652 ± 124 ms vs. 1238 ± 334 ms, main effect of coherence: F(1,17) = 65.218, p<0.001)
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-test showing effect of coherence on RT in healthy participants.

claim: In healthy participants, RT were significantly faster after speed compared to accuracy instructions (879 ± 194 ms vs. 1011 ± 219 ms).
source: and after speed compared to accuracy instructions (879 ± 194 ms vs. 1011 ± 219 ms, main effect of instruction: F(1,17) = 57.436, p<0.001, see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statistical analysis with F-test showing effect of instruction on RT in healthy participants, with reference to figure.

claim: Neither the effect of coherence nor the effect of instruction on RT differed between patients and healthy controls.
source: Importantly, neither the effect of coherence nor the effect of instruction on RT differed between patients and healthy controls when directly comparing the groups (effect of coherence t(27) = −0.793, p=0.435; effect of instruction t(27) = 0.809, p=0.425).
evidence: Statistical comparison between groups using t-tests showing no significant differences.

claim: There were no differences between patients and healthy participants regarding adjustments of decision thresholds (51% posterior probability).
source: Importantly, however, there were no differences between groups regarding adjustments of decision thresholds (51% posterior probability), that is, patients and healthy participants changed their thresholds to a similar extent between speed and accuracy instructions.
evidence: Bayesian hierarchical drift diffusion model comparison between groups showing no significant difference in threshold adjustments.

claim: STN power showed a well-known decrease in 13–30 Hz beta power around the motor response (from ~250 ms before until 250 ms after the response).
source: Aligning STN power to the onset of the motor responses showed the well-known decrease in 13–30 Hz beta power around the motor response (from ~250 ms before until 250 ms after the response), which was followed by an increase in beta power from ~500 ms until 1000 ms after the response (Figure 3A).
evidence: Description of observed STN beta power changes with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: STN beta power showed an increase from ~500 ms until 1000 ms after the response.
source: Aligning STN power to the onset of the motor responses showed the well-known decrease in 13–30 Hz beta power around the motor response (from ~250 ms before until 250 ms after the response), which was followed by an increase in beta power from ~500 ms until 1000 ms after the response (Figure 3A).
evidence: Description of observed STN beta power changes with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: STN LFO power of 2–8 Hz showed an inverse pattern to beta with a pronounced increase in power around the time of the response.
source: LFO power of 2–8 Hz showed an inverse pattern with a pronounced increase in power around the time of the response.
evidence: Description of observed STN LFO power changes.

claim: STN LFO power was significantly stronger after speed compared to accuracy instructions in the time period preceding the response (p<0.05).
source: First, when comparing speed and accuracy conditions, LFO power was significantly stronger after speed compared to accuracy instructions in the time period preceding the response (p<0.05), while there was no difference between trials with low and high coherence (p>0.05, see Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Statistical comparison using cluster-based permutation testing showing effect of instruction on STN LFO power, with reference to figures.

claim: There was no difference in STN LFO power between trials with low and high coherence (p>0.05).
source: First, when comparing speed and accuracy conditions, LFO power was significantly stronger after speed compared to accuracy instructions in the time period preceding the response (p<0.05), while there was no difference between trials with low and high coherence (p>0.05, see Figure 3B–C).
evidence: Statistical comparison using cluster-based permutation testing showing no effect of coherence on STN LFO power.

claim: The pre-response increase in STN LFO power during speed instructions was also observed when aligning the spectra to the onset of the moving dots cue with a significant cluster starting ~500 ms after dots onset (p<0.001).
source: The pre-response increase in LFO power during speed instructions was also observed when aligning the spectra to the onset of the moving dots cue with a significant cluster starting ~500 ms after dots onset (p<0.001), see Figure 4A–C.
evidence: Statistical comparison using cluster-based permutation testing showing effect of instruction on cue-aligned STN LFO power, with reference to figures.

claim: There was no significant phase consistency of LFO across trials (intertrial-phase clustering) in the cue- or response-aligned data neither after speed nor accuracy instructions (all p>0.05).
source: Furthermore, in the considered time periods, there was no significant phase consistency of LFO across trials (intertrial-phase clustering, see Material and methods) in the cue- or response-aligned data neither after speed nor accuracy instructions (all p>0.05).
evidence: Statistical analysis of intertrial phase clustering showing no significant phase consistency.

claim: The observed differences in STN LFO power did not have strong cue- or response-evoked components.
source: This indicates that the observed differences in LFO power did not have strong cue- or response-evoked components.
evidence: Inference based on lack of significant intertrial phase clustering.

claim: The cue-induced beta decrease was more pronounced after speed compared to accuracy instructions (11.8% ± 5.8% vs. 6.9% ± 3.3%).
source: ANOVA showed that the cue-induced beta decrease was more pronounced after speed compared to accuracy instructions (11.8% ± 5.8% vs. 6.9% ± 3.3%, main effect of instruction: F(1,10) = 6.619, p=0.028, Figure 4E)
evidence: Statistical analysis with ANOVA showing effect of instruction on cue-induced beta decrease, with reference to Figure 4E.

claim: There was no effect of coherence on the cue-induced beta decrease (F(1,10) = 0.177, p=0.683).
source: while there was no effect of coherence (F(1,10) = 0.177, p=0.683)
evidence: Statistical analysis with ANOVA showing no effect of coherence on cue-induced beta decrease.

claim: Single trial changes in STN LFO and beta band were not statistically related to each other (mean rho = −0.006 ± 0.042, t(10) = −0.45, p=0.662).
source: Interestingly, these single trial changes in the LFO and beta band were not statistically related to each other as indicated by correlation analysis (mean rho = −0.006 ± 0.042, t(10) = −0.45, p=0.662, visualized in Figure 5B).
evidence: Correlation analysis showing no significant relationship between STN LFO and beta power changes, with reference to Figure 5B.

claim: STN LFO power had a significant effect on decision thresholds (99% posterior probability).
source: This revealed a significant effect of LFO (99% posterior probability) as well as an interaction of LFO*instruction (95% posterior probability), see Figure 5C.
evidence: Bayesian hierarchical drift diffusion model regression analysis showing effect of LFO on thresholds, with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: There was a significant interaction of LFO*instruction on decision thresholds (95% posterior probability).
source: This revealed a significant effect of LFO (99% posterior probability) as well as an interaction of LFO*instruction (95% posterior probability), see Figure 5C.
evidence: Bayesian hierarchical drift diffusion model regression analysis showing interaction effect, with reference to Figure 5C.

claim: STN LFO predicted elevated decision thresholds only after accuracy instructions (96% posterior probability), but not after speed instructions (63% posterior probability).
source: Post-hoc tests showed that LFO predicted elevated decision thresholds only after accuracy instructions (96% posterior probability), but not after speed instructions (63% posterior probability).
evidence: Post-hoc Bayesian analysis showing context-specific effect of LFO on thresholds.

claim: Cue-induced beta power decreases predicted lower decision thresholds (95% posterior probability).
source: Cue-induced beta power decreases predicted lower decision thresholds (95% posterior probability), but there was no interaction of beta*instruction (59% posterior probability, Figure 5D).
evidence: Bayesian hierarchical drift diffusion model regression analysis showing effect of beta on thresholds, with reference to Figure 5D.

claim: There was no interaction of beta*instruction on decision thresholds (59% posterior probability).
source: Cue-induced beta power decreases predicted lower decision thresholds (95% posterior probability), but there was no interaction of beta*instruction (59% posterior probability, Figure 5D).
evidence: Bayesian hierarchical drift diffusion model regression analysis showing no interaction effect.

claim: The relationship between beta power decreases and thresholds was specific to the early cue-induced decrease in beta, since the averaged pre-response beta power did not predict threshold adjustments (54% posterior probability).
source: Importantly, the relationship between beta power decreases and thresholds was specific to the early cue-induced decrease in beta, since the averaged pre-response beta power (computed analogously to pre-response LFO power) did not predict threshold adjustments (54% posterior probability), which is in line with previous observations (Herz et al., 2016).
evidence: Bayesian hierarchical drift diffusion model regression analysis showing specificity of beta effect, with citation to previous work.

claim: There were no relationships between STN LFO or beta power changes and trial-by-trial fluctuations in drift rates.
source: This analysis showed that there were no relationships between STN LFO or beta power changes and trial-by-trial fluctuations in drift rates (effect of LFO: 69% posterior probability, LFO*coherence: 73% posterior probability, beta-decrease: 53% posterior probability, beta-decrease*coherence: 53% posterior probability).
evidence: Bayesian hierarchical drift diffusion model regression analysis showing no effects on drift rates.

claim: The HDDM incorporating STN power changes improved model performance compared to the HDDM not containing any neural data (difference in deviance information criterion: 485).
source: Finally, the HDDM incorporating STN power changes also improved model performance compared to the HDDM not containing any neural data (difference in deviance information criterion: 485).
evidence: Model comparison using deviance information criterion showing improved fit with neural data.

claim: The pre-response increase in STN LFO power predicted increased RT only after accuracy (slope: 0.038, p=0.022), but not after speed instructions (slope: −0.006, p=0.366).
source: We found that the pre-response increase in LFO power predicted increased RT only after accuracy (slope: 0.038, p=0.022), but not after speed instructions (slope: −0.006, p=0.366).
evidence: Regression analysis showing context-specific relationship between LFO and RT.

claim: Stronger cue-induced decreases in STN beta power predicted shorter RT across instructions (slope: −0.022, p=0.035).
source: In addition, stronger cue-induced decreases in beta power predicted shorter RT across instructions (slope: −0.022, p=0.035).
evidence: Regression analysis showing relationship between beta and RT.

claim: EEG activity recorded at Fz showed a stronger pre-response LFO increase compared to electrodes C3/C4 (2.7% ± 4.4% vs. −1.1 ± 1.3%, p<0.05).
source: EEG activity recorded at Fz showed a stronger pre-response LFO increase compared to electrodes C3/C4 (2.7% ± 4.4% vs. −1.1 ± 1.3%, p<0.05).
evidence: Statistical comparison using permutation testing showing spatial specificity of LFO modulation.

claim: EEG activity at C3/C4 displayed a more pronounced cue-induced decrease in beta power compared to Fz (12% ± 8% vs. 4.3% ± 1.8%, p<0.001).
source: Conversely, activity at C3/C4 displayed a more pronounced cue-induced decrease in beta power compared to Fz (12% ± 8% vs. 4.3% ± 1.8%, p<0.001).
evidence: Statistical comparison using permutation testing showing spatial specificity of beta modulation.

claim: Fz-STN ISPC in the LFO band was not significantly different between speed and accuracy instructions in the pre-response period (p>0.1).
source: Fz-STN ISPC in the LFO band was not significantly different between speed and accuracy instructions in the pre-response period (p>0.1), see Figure 6C.
evidence: Statistical comparison using permutation testing showing no difference in phase coupling between instructions, with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: Correlations between Fz-STN ISPC and STN LFO power were significantly different between speed and accuracy instructions (z(7) = −2.33, Pcorrected = 0.04).
source: However, correlations between Fz-STN ISPC and STN LFO power were significantly different between speed and accuracy instructions (z(7) = −2.33, Pcorrected = 0.04).
evidence: Statistical comparison of correlation coefficients showing context-dependent relationship.

claim: There was no relationship between Fz-STN ISPC and STN power after speed instructions (rho = −0.301, Pcorrected = 0.938).
source: While there was no relationship between Fz-STN ISPC and STN power after speed instructions (rho = −0.301, Pcorrected = 0.938), there was a significant positive correlation between Fz-STN coupling and STN power in the LFO band after accuracy instructions (rho = 0.823, Pcorrected = 0.024), see Figure 6C.
evidence: Correlation analysis showing no significant relationship after speed instructions, with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: There was a significant positive correlation between Fz-STN coupling and STN power in the LFO band after accuracy instructions (rho = 0.823, Pcorrected = 0.024).
source: While there was no relationship between Fz-STN ISPC and STN power after speed instructions (rho = −0.301, Pcorrected = 0.938), there was a significant positive correlation between Fz-STN coupling and STN power in the LFO band after accuracy instructions (rho = 0.823, Pcorrected = 0.024), see Figure 6C.
evidence: Correlation analysis showing significant positive relationship after accuracy instructions, with reference to Figure 6C.

claim: C3/C4-STN ISPC in the beta band showed a pronounced decrease after onset of the cue only after speed, but not accuracy instructions.
source: C3/C4-STN ISPC in the beta band showed a pronounced decrease after onset of the cue only after speed, but not accuracy instructions (Figure 6D), leading to a significant difference between conditions (p<0.01).
evidence: Statistical comparison using permutation testing showing effect of instruction on beta phase coupling, with reference to Figure 6D.

claim: The relationship between C3/C4-STN beta ISPC and STN beta power was significantly different between speed and accuracy instructions (z(7) = −2.65, Pcorrected = 0.016).
source: Correlation analyses revealed that the relationship between C3/C4-STN beta ISPC and STN beta power was significantly different between speed and accuracy instructions (z(7) = −2.65, Pcorrected = 0.016).
evidence: Statistical comparison of correlation coefficients showing context-dependent relationship.

claim: There was a significant positive correlation between C3/C4-STN ISPC and STN beta power after speed instructions (rho = 0.832, Pcorrected = 0.02).
source: This was driven by a significant positive correlation between C3/C4-STN ISPC and STN beta power after speed instructions (rho = 0.832, Pcorrected = 0.02), while there was no significant correlation after accuracy instructions (rho = −0.447, Pcorrected = 0.534; Figure 6D)
evidence: Correlation analysis showing significant positive relationship after speed instructions, with reference to Figure 6D.

claim: There was no significant correlation between C3/C4-STN ISPC and STN beta power after accuracy instructions (rho = −0.447, Pcorrected = 0.534).
source: This was driven by a significant positive correlation between C3/C4-STN ISPC and STN beta power after speed instructions (rho = 0.832, Pcorrected = 0.02), while there was no significant correlation after accuracy instructions (rho = −0.447, Pcorrected = 0.534; Figure 6D)
evidence: Correlation analysis showing no significant relationship after accuracy instructions, with reference to Figure 6D.

claim: Two distinct, statistically-uncorrelated mechanisms were found comprising modulations of a Fz-STN network in the LFO band and a C3/C4-STN network in the beta band.
source: In the current study, we combined recordings of STN LFP and cortical EEG during perceptual decision-making with computational modeling of the latent parameters underlying the decision process. This allowed us to demonstrate neural correlates of the involvement of STN and of cortico-STN connectivity in controlling the trade-off between fast and accurate decisions. We found two distinct, statistically-uncorrelated mechanisms comprising modulations of a Fz-STN network in the LFO band and a C3/C4-STN network in the beta band.
evidence: Summary statement of main findings based on multiple analyses presented in the study.

claim: The two cortico-STN networks differed in their cortical topography, relative timing of recruitment and spectral characteristics as well as in their precise relationship with decision thresholds.
source: These two networks differed in their cortical topography, relative timing of recruitment and spectral characteristics as well as in their precise relationship with decision thresholds.
evidence: Summary statement of differences between the two networks based on multiple analyses.

claim: The Fz-STN network predicted increased thresholds only after accuracy instructions, while the C3/C4-STN network predicted decreased thresholds irrespective of instructions, but was more strongly modulated during speed emphasis.
source: The Fz-STN network predicted increased thresholds only after accuracy instructions, while the C3/C4-STN network predicted decreased thresholds irrespective of instructions, but was more strongly modulated during speed emphasis.
evidence: Summary statement of main findings regarding the functional roles of the two networks.

claim: Optimal decision-making requires balancing fast but error-prone and more accurate but slower decisions through adjustments of decision thresholds.
source: Optimal decision-making requires balancing fast but error-prone and more accurate but slower decisions through adjustments of decision thresholds.
evidence: Statement from the abstract summarizing the theoretical framework of the study.

claim: Speed-accuracy trade-off has been studied for over a century.
source: Fast decisions come at the cost of reduced accuracy. This elementary aspect of decision-making, often referred to as speed-accuracy trade-off, has been studied for over a century (for a review see Heitz, 2014)
evidence: Historical statement with citation to review article.

claim: Speed-accuracy trade-off can be observed in a multitude of tasks and across various species including rats, non-human primates and humans.
source: and can be observed in a multitude of tasks and across various species including rats, non-human primates and humans (Bogacz et al., 2010; Forstmann et al., 2010, 2008; Hanks et al., 2014; Heitz and Schall, 2012; Ivanoff et al., 2008; Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008, 1998; Reinagel, 2013; Schouten and Bekker, 1967; Thura and Cisek, 2016; van Veen et al., 2008; Wickelgren, 1977).
evidence: Statement supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Speed-accuracy adjustments can be implemented by elevating or lowering the 'decision threshold'.
source: Mathematically, speed-accuracy adjustments can be implemented by elevating or lowering the 'decision threshold', that is, a criterion which defines when the continuous accumulation of evidence should be terminated and the option with the strongest evidence chosen (Bogacz et al., 2006; Ratcliff and McKoon, 2008).
evidence: Statement about mathematical implementation with citations to theoretical work.

claim: In neurobiological models of decision-making, modulations of decision thresholds subserving speed-accuracy trade-offs have been assigned to the basal ganglia.
source: In neurobiological models of decision-making, such modulations of decision thresholds subserving speed-accuracy trade-offs have been assigned to the basal ganglia (BG) (Bogacz et al., 2010; Frank, 2006; Lo and Wang, 2006)
evidence: Statement about neurobiological models with citations to theoretical work.

claim: The basal ganglia are connected to a wide range of decision- and movement-related cortical areas in a closed-loop fashion.
source: which are connected to a wide range of decision- and movement-related cortical areas in a closed-loop fashion (Alexander et al., 1986; Lambert et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement about basal ganglia connectivity with citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The BG exert tonic inhibition over cortical areas, which can be decreased through activation of a facilitatory, direct pathway connecting the striatum with BG output areas or increased by activation of two net inhibitory circuits passing through the subthalamic nucleus (STN).
source: Within these loops, the BG exert tonic inhibition over cortical areas, which can be decreased through activation of a facilitatory, direct pathway connecting the striatum with BG output areas or increased by activation of two net inhibitory circuits passing through the subthalamic nucleus (STN), which incorporate the indirect and hyperdirect pathways (Alexander et al., 1986; Bogacz et al., 2010; Kravitz et al., 2010).
evidence: Statement about basal ganglia circuitry with citations to anatomical and theoretical work.

claim: Increased activity of cortical neurons computing decision-related signals during speed emphasis has been observed as firing rate changes in non-human primates.
source: Increased activity of cortical neurons computing decision-related signals during speed emphasis, as predicted by this model, has been observed as firing rate changes in non-human primates (Hanks et al., 2014; Heitz and Schall, 2012; Thura and Cisek, 2016)
evidence: Statement about cortical activity with citations to electrophysiology studies in non-human primates.

claim: fMRI studies in humans have indicated increased cortical activity during speed emphasis.
source: and indicated by functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) studies in humans (Forstmann et al., 2008; Ivanoff et al., 2008; van Veen et al., 2008).
evidence: Statement about cortical activity with citations to fMRI studies in humans.

claim: fMRI studies have inferred increased activity in striatum during speed emphasis.
source: At the BG level, fMRI studies have inferred increased activity in striatum during speed emphasis (Forstmann et al., 2008; van Veen et al., 2008).
evidence: Statement about striatal activity with citations to fMRI studies.

claim: Treatment with deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the STN affects patients' ability to switch between fast and accurate decision-making.
source: An involvement of the STN has been suggested by studies showing that treatment with deep brain stimulation (DBS) of the STN affects patients' ability to switch between fast and accurate decision-making (Green et al., 2013; Pote et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement about DBS effects with citations to behavioral studies.

claim: Behavioral studies of DBS effects are non-informative regarding the neurophysiological correlates of speed-accuracy adjustments.
source: However, these behavioral studies are non-informative regarding the neurophysiological correlates of speed-accuracy adjustments.
evidence: Statement about limitations of previous behavioral studies.

claim: Electrophysiological recordings of STN LFPs and EEG have shown that LFO modulations during 'cognitive' motor tasks are mainly related to cortical PFC activity and PFC-STN connectivity.
source: Electrophysiological recordings of STN LFPs and EEG have shown that LFO modulations during 'cognitive' motor tasks are mainly related to cortical PFC activity and PFC-STN connectivity (Cavanagh et al., 2011, 2012; Cohen, 2014b; Herz et al., 2016; Pastötter et al., 2012; Zavala et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about LFO modulations with citations to previous electrophysiology studies.

claim: Changes in cortical LFO power are mainly localized in the medial PFC.
source: More specifically, Pastötter et al. (2012) demonstrated that changes in cortical LFO power are mainly localized in the medial PFC using EEG in healthy participants performing a speed-accuracy trade-off task.
evidence: Statement about cortical localization with citation to specific EEG study.

claim: Trial-by-trial variations in Fz LFO measured using EEG correlated with activity of the medial PFC measured using fMRI and both signals were related to increases in decision thresholds.
source: Furthermore, Frank et al. (2015) showed that trial-by-trial variations in Fz LFO measured using EEG correlated with activity of the medial PFC measured using fMRI and that both signals were related to increases in decision thresholds.
evidence: Statement about relationship between EEG, fMRI, and decision thresholds with citation to specific study.

claim: The PFC contributes to decision-making and modulations of the speed-accuracy trade-off.
source: These findings add to the increasing evidence that the PFC contributes to decision-making and modulations of the speed-accuracy trade-off (Aron et al., 2016; Bogacz et al., 2010; Frank, 2006; Heekeren et al., 2008).
evidence: Statement about PFC role with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Dorsomedial PFC plays a pivotal role during context-dependent adaptations of decision-making and motor control.
source: Within the PFC, mainly – albeit not exclusively - dorsomedial PFC seems to play a pivotal role during context-dependent adaptations of decision-making and motor control (Forstmann et al., 2010, 2008; Frank et al., 2015; Herz et al., 2014; Ivanoff et al., 2008; van Veen et al., 2008; Wenzlaff et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement about dorsomedial PFC role with citations to multiple studies.

claim: Dorsomedial PFC has anatomical connections to the STN via the indirect and hyperdirect pathway.
source: Importantly, dorsomedial PFC has anatomical connections to the STN via the indirect and hyperdirect pathway (Alexander et al., 1986; Aron et al., 2007; Forstmann et al., 2010; Lambert et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement about anatomical connectivity with citations to anatomical studies.

claim: PFC increases its influence over STN activity when caution is warranted.
source: These observations are in line with the idea that PFC increases its influence over STN activity when caution is warranted (Frank, 2006; Ridderinkhof et al., 2011) leading to increased decision thresholds in order to delay the response (Frank et al., 2015; Herz et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement about PFC-STN interaction with citations to theoretical and empirical work.

claim: Increased STN LFO power has been observed in trials with distracting stimuli compared to trials without such conflict in the Flanker task.
source: Further evidence for this hypothesis has been provided by previous studies assessing 'conflict' between competing responses. Using the Flanker task Zavala and colleagues (2013, 2015, 2016) found increased STN LFO power in trials with distracting stimuli compared to trials without such conflict.
evidence: Statement about STN LFO in conflict tasks with citations to specific studies.

claim: Similar changes in STN LFO power have been observed during a Stroop task.
source: Similar changes in STN LFO power have been observed during a Stroop task (Brittain et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement about STN LFO in Stroop task with citation to specific study.

claim: Response conflict has been shown to increase decision thresholds.
source: Since response conflict has been shown to increase decision thresholds (Ratcliff and Frank, 2012), these previously reported LFO changes might be related to threshold adjustments.
evidence: Statement about conflict effects on thresholds with citation, used to interpret previous findings.

claim: LFO activity measured over PFC using EEG is modulated by various processes including novelty, punishment, error, memory and learning.
source: However, LFO activity – at least when measured over PFC using EEG - cannot be simply mapped to one specific process or mechanism, since it is not only modulated by conflict, but various processes including novelty, punishment, error, memory and learning (Cavanagh et al., 2012; Cohen, 2014b).
evidence: Statement about multiple functional roles of LFO with citations to review articles.

claim: Beta power modulations during movements have been localized to motor areas.
source: At the cortical level, beta power modulations during movements (Pape and Siegel, 2016; Pfurtscheller, 1981; 2003), decision-making (Donner et al., 2009; Wyart et al., 2012) and speed-accuracy trade-offs (Pastötter et al., 2012) have been localized to motor areas.
evidence: Statement about cortical localization of beta modulations with citations to multiple studies.

claim: STN beta oscillations are coherent to motor cortical areas during rest.
source: Furthermore, STN beta oscillations are coherent to motor cortical areas during rest (Hirschmann et al., 2011; Litvak et al., 2011).
evidence: Statement about STN-motor cortex coherence with citations to connectivity studies.

claim: 'Decision-related' signals can be observed in areas involved in motor preparation and execution.
source: Thus, even though conclusive evidence can only be provided through simultaneous STN and focal cortical recordings, for example, using electrocorticography, the observed beta band changes in STN and at C3/C4 in the current study are likely to be related to modulations of a motor cortical-STN network adding to the increasing evidence that 'decision-related' signals can be observed in areas involved in motor preparation and execution (Cisek and Kalaska, 2010; Donner et al., 2009; Klein-Flügge and Bestmann, 2012; Pastötter et al., 2012; Thura and Cisek, 2016).
evidence: Statement about decision-related signals in motor areas with citations to multiple studies.

claim: The BG and variations in STN beta power are related to encoding movement vigor.
source: In the current study, we did not measure movement velocity or force. However, previous studies have provided strong evidence that the BG in general (Desmurget and Turner, 2010; Yttri and Dudman, 2016), and variations in STN beta power in particular (Tan et al., 2015, 2016), are related to encoding movement vigor.
evidence: Statement about BG and STN beta role in movement vigor with citations to previous studies.

claim: During speed-accuracy adjustments speed emphasis not only decreases decision times, but also increases movement vigor to indicate the choice.
source: During speed-accuracy adjustments speed emphasis not only decreases decision times, but also increases movement vigor to indicate the choice (Spieser et al., 2016; Thura et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about speed-accuracy effects on movement vigor with citations to previous studies.

claim: The longer is spent on deliberation the less time is spent on performing the motor response.
source: Furthermore, the longer is spent on deliberation the less time is spent on performing the motor response (Thura and Cisek, 2016; Thura et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about relationship between deliberation and motor execution time with citations to previous studies.

claim: A common signal might underlie adjustments in the speed of decision and vigor of movements.
source: Such close relationships between 'cognitive' and 'motor' aspects of a decision have led to the hypothesis that a common signal might underlie adjustments in the speed of decision and vigor of movements (Thura and Cisek, 2016; Thura et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about hypothesis linking decision speed and movement vigor with citations to theoretical work.

claim: When speed is emphasized, neurons integrating sensory evidence exhibit an increase in the baseline and gain of firing rates during deliberation, rather than terminating at lower levels of firing rates before the choice is executed.
source: Recordings of cortical single-unit activity in non-human primates have shown that when speed is emphasized, neurons integrating sensory evidence exhibit an increase in the baseline and gain of firing rates during deliberation, rather than terminating at lower levels of firing rates before the choice is executed (Hanks et al., 2014; Heitz and Schall, 2012; Thura and Cisek, 2016).
evidence: Statement about neural mechanisms of speed-accuracy adjustments with citations to electrophysiology studies in non-human primates.

claim: A shift in baseline, but not a change in the threshold, underlies speed-accuracy adjustments at the neural level.
source: These findings indicate that a shift in baseline, but not a change in the threshold (which is mathematically equivalent, see also Figure 2A), underlies speed-accuracy adjustments at the neural level.
evidence: Interpretation of previous findings with reference to Figure 2A showing mathematical equivalence.

claim: Changes in cortical activity and excitability could be mediated through the BG by modulating tonic feedback inhibition of the cortex.
source: Such changes in cortical activity and excitability could be mediated through the BG by modulating tonic feedback inhibition of the cortex (Alexander et al., 1986; Bogacz et al., 2010; Kravitz et al., 2010) putatively in the form of a dynamic 'urgency' signal (Churchland et al., 2008; Cisek and Kalaska, 2010; Drugowitsch et al., 2012; Thura and Cisek, 2016; Thura et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about potential mechanism with citations to anatomical and theoretical work.

claim: Changes in cortical firing rates during speed-accuracy adjustments have been observed in multiple areas comprising motor and premotor cortex, parietal cortex and frontal eye field.
source: Interestingly, changes in cortical firing rates during speed-accuracy adjustments have been observed in multiple areas comprising motor and premotor cortex (Thura and Cisek, 2016), parietal cortex (Hanks et al., 2014) and frontal eye field (Heitz and Schall, 2012), all of which share connections with the STN (Lambert et al., 2012).
evidence: Statement about widespread cortical changes with citations to multiple electrophysiology studies and anatomical work.

claim: Context-dependent changes in STN activity could adjust cortical activity simultaneously in multiple, spatially remote areas according to current task demands.
source: Thus, context-dependent changes in STN activity could adjust cortical activity (e.g. baseline firing rates) simultaneously in multiple, spatially remote areas according to current task demands.
evidence: Inference based on anatomical connectivity and observed activity patterns.

claim: Neural activity changes within the basal ganglia during speed-accuracy trade-offs are not limited to the STN.
source: As mentioned earlier, cortex and basal ganglia are interconnected through circuits, which comprise not only cortico–STN connections, but involve a multitude of subcortical areas (Alexander et al., 1986; Kravitz et al., 2010; Lambert et al., 2012). Therefore, we do not assume that during speed-accuracy trade-offs neural activity changes within the basal ganglia are limited to the STN.
evidence: Statement about broader basal ganglia involvement with citations to anatomical work.

claim: Spike-based communication can be optimized regarding efficiency and selectivity through synchronized oscillations.
source: Since spike-based communication can be optimized regarding efficiency and selectivity through synchronized oscillations (Fries, 2015), we propose that the changes in oscillatory activity observed in this study reflect modulations of distinct neural communication channels facilitating adjustments between hasty and cautious decision regimes.
evidence: Statement about oscillatory communication with citation to theoretical work, used to interpret findings.

claim: Distinct mechanisms are employed in the brain to facilitate speed-accuracy adjustments in cortico-basal ganglia networks.
source: Together, our results suggest that distinct mechanisms are employed in the brain to facilitate speed-accuracy adjustments in cortico-basal ganglia networks.
evidence: Summary statement of main conclusion based on all findings.

claim: All patients were tested on their normal dopaminergic medication.
source: In order to approximate physiological STN function as well as possible all patients were tested on their normal dopaminergic medication.
evidence: Direct statement about medication status during testing.

claim: All patients had a good dopamine response as indicated by a pronounced improvement of motor function after a levodopa challenge in the preoperative assessment (mean improvement in Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale-III 61.9% ± 12.6).
source: All patients had a good dopamine response as indicated by a pronounced improvement of motor function after a levodopa challenge in the preoperative assessment (mean improvement in Unified Parkinson's Disease Rating Scale-III 61.9% ± 12.6, see supplementary file 1).
evidence: Clinical data about patients' dopamine responsiveness.

claim: Decision thresholds are not modulated by dopamine in healthy people.
source: Of note, decision thresholds - the main interest of the current study – are not modulated by dopamine in healthy people (Winkel et al., 2012) or PD patients (Huang et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement about dopamine effects on decision thresholds with citations to previous studies.

claim: Decision thresholds are not modulated by dopamine in PD patients.
source: Of note, decision thresholds - the main interest of the current study – are not modulated by dopamine in healthy people (Winkel et al., 2012) or PD patients (Huang et al., 2015).
evidence: Statement about dopamine effects on decision thresholds with citations to previous studies.

evidence: Direct statement about experimental setup with citation to software.

source: While trials with different coherence levels were randomly interspersed, accuracy and speed trials alternated in blocks of 20 trials (Green et al., 2013).

claim: The blocks were repeated six times each resulting in 240 trials for the whole experiment.
source: These blocks were repeated six times each resulting in 240 trials for the whole experiment (Figure 1B), which lasted approximately 10 min.

claim: The experiment lasted approximately 10 min.

source: We recorded bilateral STN LFPs from the implanted DBS electrodes.

source: Additionally, in 8 of the 11 patients, electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded over two regions of interest: dorsomedial prefrontal cortex (PFC) and motor cortex areas.

source: Data were sampled at 2048 Hz, band-pass filtered between 0.5 and 500 Hz and amplified (TMSi porti, TMS International, Enschede, The Netherlands).
evidence: Direct statement about data acquisition parameters.

claim: Artifacts related to eye movements were removed by subtracting the filtered and adaptively scaled EOG data.
source: Artifacts related to eye movements were removed by subtracting the filtered and adaptively scaled EOG data (40 Hz low-pass filter).
evidence: Direct statement about artifact removal procedure.

claim: Data were downsampled to 200 Hz, high-pass filtered at 1 Hz and low-pass filtered at 100 Hz.
source: Data were downsampled to 200 Hz, high-pass filtered at 1 Hz and low-pass filtered at 100 Hz.
evidence: Direct statement about data preprocessing.

claim: Power and phase of LFPs were computed using the continuous wavelet transform with two cycles per frequency for the lowest considered frequency (2 Hz) which linearly increased to five cycles per frequency for the highest considered frequency (30 Hz) in 1 Hz steps.
source: Power and phase of LFPs were computed using the continuous wavelet transform with two cycles per frequency for the lowest considered frequency (2 Hz) which linearly increased to five cycles per frequency for the highest considered frequency (30 Hz) in 1 Hz steps.

claim: In 53% of hemispheres, the bipolar channel showing the strongest beta modulation was identical to the channel showing the strongest LFO modulation.
source: In 53% of hemispheres, the bipolar channel showing the strongest beta modulation was identical to the channel showing the strongest LFO modulation and in 47% the best LFO channel was localized ventrally to the best beta channel.
evidence: Direct statement about spatial relationship between beta and LFO modulation.

claim: In 47% of hemispheres the best LFO channel was localized ventrally to the best beta channel.
source: In 53% of hemispheres, the bipolar channel showing the strongest beta modulation was identical to the channel showing the strongest LFO modulation and in 47% the best LFO channel was localized ventrally to the best beta channel.

source: We applied 1000 permutations and used p=0.05 as cluster-building threshold and as statistical threshold for cluster-based comparisons.
evidence: Direct statement about statistical analysis method.

source: We also compared differences between error and correct trials for the low coherence condition. This control analysis showed no significant differences and is shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.
evidence: Statement about control analysis results with reference to supplementary figure.

claim: The hierarchical design of HDDM assumes that parameters from individual participants are not completely independent, but drawn from the group distribution while allowing variations from this distribution given sufficient evidence to overwhelm the group prior.
source: The hierarchical design assumes that parameters from individual participants are not completely independent, but drawn from the group distribution while allowing variations from this distribution given sufficient evidence to overwhelm the group prior.

source: Markov chain Monte Carlo sampling was used for Bayesian approximation of the posterior distribution of model parameters generating 20,000 samples and discarding 10,000 samples as burn-in (Herz et al., 2016).

evidence: Statement about data exclusion criterion for HDDM analysis with rationale.

source: Posteriors of regression coefficients for trial-wise regressors were estimated only at the group level to address potential collinearity among model parameters, for regularizing parameter estimates and to prevent parameter explosion (Frank et al., 2015; Wiecki et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement about modeling approach with citations to methodological papers.

claim: DIC is mainly used for comparisons of hierarchical models where other measures, such as the Bayesian information criterion (BIC), are not appropriate.
source: DIC is mainly used for comparisons of hierarchical models where other measures, such as the Bayesian information criterion (BIC), are not appropriate (Frank et al., 2015; Wiecki et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement about model comparison metric with citations.

claim: DIC differences >10 are traditionally considered significant.
source: Traditionally, DIC differences >10 are considered significant (Herz et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement about interpretation of DIC with citation.

claim: ISPC is a phase-based measure of connectivity reflecting to what extent oscillations in two different areas are phase-locked at specific time points.
source: ISPC is a phase-based measure of connectivity reflecting to what extent oscillations in two different areas are phase-locked at specific time points (Cohen, 2014a; Herz et al., 2016; Zavala et al., 2013, 2014, 2016).
evidence: Statement about connectivity measure with citations to methodological papers.

claim: ISPC is independent of power changes in that it only considers the phase information of the signal.
source: This measure is independent of power changes in that it only considers the phase information of the signal and will be only affected by power in cases where power is very low (because phase estimates deteriorate) or zero (because phase cannot be estimated with zero power) (Cohen, 2014a).
evidence: Statement about properties of connectivity measure with citation.

claim: Single subject estimates of decision thresholds were not used for any correlation analyses, since the hierarchical design of HDDM violates the assumption of independence of observations.
source: Please note that single subject estimates of decision thresholds were not used for any correlation analyses, since the hierarchical design of HDDM violates the assumption of independence of observations (Wiecki et al., 2013).
evidence: Statement about analysis constraint with citation to methodological paper.
